summary:
Two satellites watch fires, but they do not count the same way. MODIS sees 1 km pixels since 2000; VIIRS sees 375 m pixels since 2012. 
In Quebec in 2023, VIIRS counted 231,500 hotspots and MODIS only 32,648 — 7.09 times more, not because there was 7 times more fire, but because VIIRS is sharper. 

Our web app harmonizes the two records into one burning activity calendar for Quebec, Yellowknife and Angola, using NASA FIRMS data only. 
We group VIIRS points in the same 1 km cell on the same day as one fire. The gap falls from 7.09 to 3.09 in Quebec (F = 3.19), and from 3.46 to 2.29 in Angola (F = 2.40). 
F = calibration factor, the VIIRS / MODIS ratio after 1 km/day grouping, in peak months.

Why two different F?
Because the fires are different. In Quebec, forest fires, big and hot. In Angola, many small agricultural fires. So each region needs its own F. We never use Quebec 3.19 for Angola, and never use Angola 2.40 for Quebec.

The calendar shows the truth in one second: June 2023 in Quebec had 53,081 harmonized hotspots — 81 times June 2022; August 2023 in Angola had 229,359. 
The app is built for firefighters: a simple morning briefing in French and English, with a level Normal, Watch, High, Critical, a colour calendar for 2020–2025, charts, CSV downloads and a one-page PDF, no install, no email notifications.

I confirm this is original work by Team 810 Atossa, using public NASA FIRMS data and published fire detection methods as requested by the challenge.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Two satellites watch fires, but they do not count the same way.

MODIS sees 1 km pixels since 2000. VIIRS sees 375 m pixels since 2012.

In Quebec in 2023, VIIRS counted 231,500 hotspots and MODIS only 32,648, a raw ratio of 7.09 times. That is not 7 times more fire, it is a sharper sensor.

Our web app, Burning Activity Calendar — Canada and Angola, harmonizes the two records into one calendar, using NASA FIRMS data only.

Method:

1) Clean both sensors the same way, MODIS confidence 30 or more, VIIRS nominal / high only.

2) Group all hotspots in the same 1 km cell on the same day as 1 fire, for both sensors.

3) Calibrate on the overlap period. In Quebec the clustered VIIRS / MODIS ratio is 3.01 in June, 3.23 in July and 3.19 in August 2023, so the calibration factor F = 3.19. In Angola F = 2.40. Each region has its own F, never reused.

4) The harmonized series from 2012 is VIIRS grouped to 1 km per day. Before 2012, MODIS grouped times F estimates what VIIRS would have seen. MODIS and VIIRS are never added together, and Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 VIIRS are never added together.

Results:

Quebec harmonized totals, for the whole year, January to December, whole province of Quebec, in 1 km cell per day units:

2020: 2,284, of which June 794;

2021: 2,666, of which July 1,046;

2022: 2,067, of which June 655;

2023: 85,162, of which June 53,081;

2024: 4,349, of which June 1,976;

2025: 2,247, of which August 567.

A fire burning several days, over several 1 km squares, counts once per day and once per square. June 2023 was 53,081, 81 times June 2022, level Critical.

Yellowknife, box around the city:

2020: 0;

2021: 3;

2022: 1,371;

2023: 16,660, August 8,662;

2024: 305;

2025: 8,632.

August 2023 in Yellowknife was not just a number in our calendar. It was a real evacuation of a whole city, Really hell! Our number for Yellowknife, August 2023, 8,662 harmonized hotspots, July 7,066, total 2023 16,660. In normal years, Yellowknife is 0, 3, 305.

What happened in real life, in August 2023:

· Some 20,000 people have been ordered to evacuate their homes in Yellowknife, the capital of Canada's Northwest Territories, and the surrounding areas as the Behchoko/Yellowknife wildfire burns out of control less than 10 miles outside the city.

· About 20,000 people, the entire population of Yellowknife, were ordered to evacuate by noon Friday as a wildfire threatened the city.

· The evacuation order was issued on Wednesday 16 August 2023, residents had until noon Friday to leave, by car on the only highway out, and by plane.

· More than 230 active fires were threatening other cities and towns in the region, and 265 fires in the Northwest Territories that year.

So, 8,662 is not a bug in our calculation. It is the satellite record of a hell month, when a whole city had to flee.

That is exactly why we chose Yellowknife — a city on Yellowknives Dene First Nation land in the Northwest Territories — to compare with the province of Quebec.

Quebec June 2023 was 53,081, Yellowknife August 2023 was 8,662, and both were Critical, but in different months, for different places.

Angola, whole country:

2020: 665,862;

2021: 687,816;

2022: 585,065;

2023: 747,709, August 229,359;

2024: 726,673;

2025: 686,558.

Grand total 4,099,683. Fire season in Angola is May to October, every year, with no single outlier year like Quebec 2023.

The app: choose Quebec, Yellowknife or Angola, pick a year and a month, and get a morning briefing, harmonized number, alert level Normal / Watch / High / Critical, and comparison with the other five years.

Colour calendar 2020-2025, with Harmonized / MODIS raw / VIIRS raw switch, log-scale chart, harmonization explained in plain words, sensor timeline, CSV downloads, and a one-page PDF briefing. Bilingual English / French. No login required to use the app, no install.

Why these three regions?

We chose Quebec, Yellowknife and Angola on purpose, to test the same method in three very different places.

Quebec is my homeland, a province in Canada, with boreal forest. In 2023 it had an extreme fire year: 85,162 harmonized hotspots, June 2023 alone 53,081, 81 times June 2022. It shows the App can see a normal year and an exceptional year.

Yellowknife is a city in the Northwest Territories, on Yellowknives Dene First Nation land, with a very high fire risk. In August 2023, about 20,000 people had to evacuate the city, 16-18 August 2023. Our calendar shows August 2023: 8,662 harmonized hotspots. It shows the App can work at the scale of a city, not only a whole province, and for a real emergency that people lived through.

Angola is a country in Africa, one of the countries with the highest numbers of fires in the world, mostly agricultural and savanna fires in the dry season, May to October. NASA reported 61,661 VIIRS fire alerts in Angola in one week, 18-25 June 2020, with 102,738 in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the same week. Angola had 747,709 harmonized hotspots in 2023, and 585,065 to 747,709 every year, 2020-2025, with no single outlier year. It shows the App can work in a savanna, not only in a boreal forest, and in a place with fire every year.

Together, the three regions show the same method, the same NASA FIRMS data, the same 1 km cell per day grouping, working on two continents, in a boreal forest and in a savanna, in a province, a city and a country. Fire is a shared human problem, not a local problem. That is the international spirit of this work: one simple tool, in French and in English, that any fire service can use, in Canada and in Angola, to see in 30 seconds if a month is normal or exceptional.

What benefits does it have, and what is the intended impact?

FIRMS and its Web Fire Mapper show where fires are today, as points on a map. They do not harmonize MODIS and VIIRS into one number, they do not show a month-by-month calendar for 2020-2025, and they do not say whether a month is normal or exceptional. Our app turns FIRMS data into that answer in 30 seconds, in French or English, with a one-page PDF for the team.

It is built for firefighters and fire services in Canada, especially volunteer fire services represented by Canadian Volunteer Fire Services Association (CVFSA). The author is a volunteer for CVFSA.

A fire team can check in the morning: is this month normal, or exceptional, and how does it compare to the last five years? That helps planning, preparation, and talking to the public, before the fire season, and during it. No email notifications, the user opens the app when needed, nothing fills the inbox. The same method works for Angola, and can be reused for other provinces and regions.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Coding languages: Python, HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No Java, no other programming language.

Data processing in Python, with pandas and NumPy: filter_quebec_2023.py, harmonize_2023.py, process_year.py, process_yellowknife.py and process_angola.py. The scripts filter the NASA FIRMS Archive CSV files by bounding box and confidence, group hotspots in the same 1 km cell on the same day as one count, and produce the harmonized monthly CSV files for 2020-2025.

Web app in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in one single HTML file: morning briefing, colour calendar 2020-2025, log-scale chart, harmonization explanation, sensor timeline, and a one-page PDF briefing button with a built-in PDF writer, no external library. No server, no database, no install, no login. It runs in a normal web browser, on a laptop first, and simple on a phone.

Data: NASA FIRMS only — MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS Suomi NPP Collection 2, Archive CSV files for Canada and Angola. A FIRMS MAP_KEY was used only for a small Near Real-Time test, Quebec 10-13 November 2026, and is not in the code.

Other tools: Muse, the AI assistant used to build the app, disclosed below; Google Drive, to store the FIRMS files; GitHub, for backup of the code and small CSV files, not required for the judges; Microsoft PowerPoint, to make the 7-slide demo; OpenAI ChatGPT, only to create the team image, disclosed below.

Hardware: an ordinary laptop, no special hardware, no satellite hardware.

How is your project creative?

It does not show another map of points. It turns two different satellite records into one comparable number, and then into a simple calendar and a morning briefing a firefighter can read in 30 seconds. The title changes with the country chosen, Canada or Angola, the subtitle shows only the chosen region, and the app is bilingual, laptop first and simple on a phone.

What factors did your team consider?

Quality Assurance, software reliability, and risk management.

1. Data reliability — NASA FIRMS only.

We used only the data given by the challenge, NASA FIRMS, MODIS Collection 6.1, 1 km, since 2000, and VIIRS Collection 2, 375 m, since 2012. No other dataset, no burned area product. Archive files for history, 2 to 3 months delay, Near Real-Time, under 3 hours, only for today. We checked the files we used: 24 files, Canada and Angola, 2020-2025, MODIS and VIIRS Suomi NPP. 72 files in our Drive were not used. We state honest gaps: VIIRS Suomi NPP archive is missing days in July 2024, 20 of 31 days, and August 2022, 21 of 31 days, in Angola, and MODIS 2021 ends 14 December 2021. We do not fill missing days. Suomi NPP stopped delivering new data on 2 November 2026, VIIRS continuity is NOAA-20 / NOAA-21, same sensor, 375 m.

Clouds and missing data: a FIRMS hotspot CSV lists fire pixels only, it does not say if a day was cloudy or if data were missing. A day with 0 fires could be no fire, fire hidden by cloud, or no data. We work by month, not by day, because the MODIS guide says intervals under about 8 days are severely biased. We count distinct days in our own files, and we cross-check MODIS and VIIRS. Clouds hide fires, they do not create them, so our totals are a minimum, not an overcount. After the competition, we will check the FIRMS missing data table, and use Level 3 / CMG products, which count cloud, clear land and missing pixels.

2. Algorithm reliability — harmonization, double-counting, and false fires.

Cleaning: MODIS confidence 30 or more, VIIRS nominal / high only, bounding box first. Grouping: 1 km cell per day, 1 count per cell per day. Harmonized from 2012 is VIIRS grouped only. MODIS and VIIRS are never added together. Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 VIIRS are never added together for the calendar. A fire burning 5 days counts once per day, a fire covering 10 squares counts once per square, by design.

Calibration factor F is per region, never reused: Quebec F = 3.19, Angola F = 2.40, Yellowknife clustered ratio 6.25 in 2023. We do not calibrate on low-fire months or years, ratios are unstable when fires are few.

FRP, Fire Radiative Power, in MW, is heat power at the satellite pass, not hectares, not temperature. Per point, MODIS is higher than VIIRS, about 126 MW vs 15 MW in Quebec 2023, because a 1 km pixel aggregates more heat. In total, they are close: Quebec 2023, MODIS 4,120,292 MW, VIIRS 3,373,102 MW.

False fires we considered: super-heated smoke plumes at night, which can create false detections several km away, especially VIIRS; lunar calibration maneuvers, about once a month, when the satellite rolls to look at the Moon, which can create linear stripes of false fires, a bug in MODIS Collection 5, fixed in Collection 6.1, which we use; static sources, factories or gas flares, which burn every day all year; volcanoes, MODIS and VIIRS detect them, but there is no active volcano in Quebec, Yellowknife or Angola, Canada's active volcanoes are in British Columbia and Yukon only, so impact is zero for our regions; bow-tie duplicate pixels in VIIRS, QA bit 22, our grouping helps for counts, but FRP sums do not use that flag, a known small risk. We do not filter by view angle, day/night, or persistence in this version, we state it, and the next step after the competition is a daily spike check, a plume / scan-angle filter, and a static-source check.

Location: a hotspot is the centre of a 375 m VIIRS or 1 km MODIS pixel, not exact GPS, data lag up to about 3 hours, satellites pass only 2 to 3 times per day, clouds can hide a fire. Ground verification is still needed. Our app is a historical calendar, 2020-2025, saying whether a month is normal or exceptional, not a live dispatch map. A live today map, with Near Real-Time and Ultra Real-Time, under 60 seconds for the US and Canada, is a post-competition step, tested with our MAP_KEY, 10-13 November 2026.

3. Software reliability — the app must work for a firefighter, in 30 seconds.

Bilingual English / French, French as default, simple words, no jargon. Laptop first, big calendar and chart, mobile simple, morning briefing first, no install, no login required to use the app. No email notifications, the user opens the app when needed, nothing fills the inbox. Colour calendar, alert levels Normal / Watch / High / Critical, CSV downloads, one-page PDF briefing. We verified the app after every change: Quebec June 2023 53,081, Yellowknife August 2023 8,662, Angola August 2023 229,359, all unchanged after Angola, after the footer, after the copyright. We fixed the PDF button when you tested it: first it did nothing, because the external library was blocked, then it needed a right-click, now one normal left-click opens the PDF in a new tab. That is software reliability: test with a real user, fix, test again, share again at the same link.

4. Risk management — do not break the app before the deadline.

Before adding Angola, we made a backup of the app, the submission pack and the demo deck. We added Angola step by step, with the same method, same code, and checked the numbers before and after. Before the submission deadline, Sunday 15 November 2026, 23:59 local time, only risk-free changes: if a change carries a risk, leave it as is, if it is possible without risk, do it completely. Public sharing was on hold until you said yes, on 15 November 2026. The demo PDF must be re-printed after every change to the deck, before uploading it. Large FIRMS files, 26 MB to 141 MB each, about 1 GB in total, are not put on GitHub, GitHub refuses files over 100 MB, only small CSVs, code and method are on GitHub.

5. Ethics, originality, and honesty.

This work is original, built by Team 810 Atossa for this challenge, from public NASA FIRMS data, with Muse, an AI assistant, to help write code and explanations, disclosed in Question 5. No NASA logo was generated or used, only the official NASA Space Apps Challenge logo in the demo. No copyrighted material was used without permission.

Copyright: © 2026 Team 810 Atossa, All rights reserved. We state our limits honestly in the app and in the submission, and we do not claim the app replaces 911, dispatch, or ground verification.
